title: .NET Core
cards/0/title: Not a new Framework version, but a new .NET
cards/0/body: Framework could not be changed: all of Windows shares it. So .NET Core was built as a separate platform. The team kept the best parts, rewrote a lot and dropped the rest.
cards/1/body:
Cross-platform: Windows, Linux, macOS.
Side-by-side versions: .NET 6, 8 and 10 live on one machine, and each app uses its own.
Self-contained: you can ship the runtime with your app.
The dotnet command: dotnet new, dotnet build, dotnet run.
Speed: release after release, .NET Core gets noticeably faster than Framework.
cards/2/task: Follow the path of .NET Core: 1.0 (2016), 2.0 (2017) and 3.x (2019).
cards/3/body:
Some parts of Framework never made it into Core:

AppDomain (isolation inside a process) → AssemblyLoadContext.
.NET Remoting → gRPC and HTTP.
WCF server → gRPC or the community-run CoreWCF.
ASP.NET Web Forms → Razor Pages and Blazor.

WPF and WinForms came back in .NET Core 3.0, but only on Windows.
cards/4/q: One server needs apps on both .NET 8 and .NET 10. What is the problem?
cards/4/options/0: None: versions install side by side, and each app uses its own
cards/4/explain: That is the difference from Framework, where 4.8 replaces 4.5.
cards/5/q: Match the old thing to its replacement
cards/6/q: What can .NET Core do that Framework could not? Select all that apply.
cards/6/options/1: Install several versions side by side
cards/6/options/2: Ship the runtime together with the app
cards/7/q: Does WPF on .NET 8 run on Linux?
cards/7/options/0: No, WPF and WinForms in modern .NET are Windows-only
cards/7/explain: For cross-platform UI, there are Avalonia and MAUI.
